do we need custom theories to explain language acquisition?

created 2026-09-13 updated 2026-09-13

Traditional research seems to assume that language acquisition is somehow special; different from other skill acquisition. Thus critical period, universal grammar, poverty of stimulus.

Yet, what parts of language learning can we actually not explain with run-of-the-mill learning theory?

  • Efficacy of comprehensible input meshes with findings in the field of perceptual skill acquisition
  • The fact that explaining someone a complex grammar rule is ineffective if the goal is to speak fluently but may help getting started seems to perfectly mirror findings (and teacher's wisdom) on how to teach procedural skills (e.g. backhand in tennis)
  • Children being able to correctly form sentence they could have never heard is not any more bewildering than firefighters being effective in fighting fires in buildings they have never seen
  • The critical period suspiciously smells like an ideal learning environment à la Deliberate Practice
    • high intrinsic base motivation: child must communicate or (e.g.) starve to death
    • massive amount of practice hours over several years
    • immediate feedback: child gets rich and detailed impression whether it was understood; what effect its communication had
    • challenged to perform at edge of ability all the time: child is constantly exposed to speech that is worth understanding as best as it currently can, but caretakers also adjust their speech so communication can occur

Just musing here. Very hard to find one's way in the decades of applied-linguistics research with its love for frameworks and meta-frameworks entirely disconnected from reality.
